```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
pal <- c(navy = "#2b3a67", teal = "#2a9d8f", orange = "#e76f51",
         gold = "#e9c46a", grey = "#bbbbbb")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 15))

res <- "results"
cs <- read_csv("../4-differential/results/contrast_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
n_comm <- cs$n_sig[cs$contrast == "genes_by_community"]
person <- read_csv(file.path(res, "scores_per_person.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
per_sample <- read_csv(file.path(res, "scores_per_sample.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
models <- read_csv(file.path(res, "model_comparison.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, c("microbiome only", "host only", "both")))
rocs <- read_csv(file.path(res, "roc_curves.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, c("microbiome only", "host only", "both")))
ranking <- read_csv(file.path(res, "predictor_ranking.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
spls_scores <- read_csv(file.path(res, "spls_scores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
module_cor <- read_csv(file.path(res, "spls_module_cor.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
stability <- read_csv(file.path(res, "spls_stability.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
diablo_cv <- read_csv(file.path(res, "diablo_cv.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
diablo_design <- read_csv(file.path(res, "diablo_design.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
diablo_load <- read_csv(file.path(res, "diablo_loadings.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
shuffle_scores <- read_csv(file.path(res, "shuffle_scores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
shuffle_cv <- read_csv(file.path(res, "shuffle_cv.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

auc_of <- function(m) sprintf("%.2f", models$auc[models$model == m])
cv_of <- function(m) sprintf("%.2f", diablo_cv$auc[diablo_cv$model == m])
mcol <- c(`microbiome only` = pal[["teal"]], `host only` = pal[["orange"]], both = pal[["navy"]])
ocol <- c(preterm = pal[["orange"]], term = pal[["navy"]])

# Draw a DAG from a node table (name, x, y, label, kind) and an edge table
# (from, to, and optionally style and label). Arrows stop short of the boxes.
kind_fill <- c(measured = pal[["teal"]], unmeasured = "#d9d9d9",
               outcome = pal[["orange"]], latent = pal[["gold"]])
kind_text <- c(measured = "white", unmeasured = "grey20", outcome = "white", latent = "grey20")
draw_dag <- function(nodes, edges, wx = 0.7, wy = 0.4, text_size = 6.2) {
  if (!"style" %in% names(edges)) edges$style <- "solid"
  if (!"label" %in% names(edges)) edges$label <- NA_character_
  e <- edges |>
    left_join(nodes |> select(from = name, x, y), by = "from") |>
    left_join(nodes |> select(to = name, xend = x, yend = y), by = "to") |>
    # stop each arrow at the edge of a box of half-width wx, half-height wy
    mutate(dx = xend - x, dy = yend - y,
           f = pmin(if_else(dx == 0, Inf, wx / abs(dx)), if_else(dy == 0, Inf, wy / abs(dy))),
           x0 = x + dx * f, y0 = y + dy * f, x1 = xend - dx * f, y1 = yend - dy * f)
  ggplot() +
    geom_segment(data = e, aes(x0, y0, xend = x1, yend = y1, linetype = style),
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.22, "cm"), type = "closed"),
                 colour = "grey35", linewidth = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_label(data = filter(e, !is.na(label)),
               aes((x0 + x1) / 2, (y0 + y1) / 2, label = label),
               size = text_size * 0.8, label.size = 0, fill = "white", colour = "grey20") +
    geom_label(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = label, fill = kind, colour = kind),
               size = text_size, lineheight = 0.9, label.padding = unit(0.35, "lines"),
               label.size = 0) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = kind_fill, name = NULL) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = kind_text, guide = "none") +
    scale_linetype_identity() +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.1)) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.08)) +
    guides(fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(label = "    "))) +
    theme_void(base_size = 16) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```

# Why integrate?

## So far, one table at a time {.center}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4
week <- tribble(
  ~day, ~what,
  "Tue AM", "shape, depth, filtering",
  "Tue PM", "distances and ordination",
  "Wed PM", "differential testing",
  "Thu PM", "sets and enrichment"
) |>
  mutate(x = row_number())
week |>
  cross_join(tibble(tbl = c("species table", "gene table"), y = c(2, 1))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = tbl), width = 0.92, height = 0.85, colour = "white", linewidth = 2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = tbl), colour = "white", size = 8) +
  geom_text(data = week, aes(x, 2.95, label = paste0(day, "\n", what)),
            size = 6.5, lineheight = 0.95, colour = "grey20") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`species table` = pal[["teal"]], `gene table` = pal[["orange"]]),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.5, 3.5)) +
  theme_void()
```

We ran every method this week twice, once on each table. Today we ask when to
use both at once.

## Questions that sound like they need both tables {.your-turn}

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}
1. Does BV cause inflammation in the cervix?
2. Which bacteria go with which host genes?
3. Can I predict preterm birth better with both tables?
4. Are there types of participants who look different in both the microbiome and the host?
5. Is the host response the reason *Gardnerella* matters?
6. Which genes are different in women with BV?
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
Sort them: **predict**, **find shared patterns**, **explain a mechanism**, or
**a one-table question**.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(3, left = 0, right = NULL, play_sound = TRUE)
```

## Kinds of question, and where we cover them

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}
| the question is about | reach for | today |
|---|---|---|
| comparing groups | one table at a time, grouped by the other | next |
| explaining a mechanism | a causal diagram first, then often a different study | DAGs |
| finding features that move together | CCA, PLS | mixOmics |
| what is shared, and what belongs to one table | MOFA | MOFA |
| types of people who look alike in every table | STATIS, mixKernel, SNF | people, not features |
| predicting an outcome | scores in one model, DIABLO | DIABLO |

: {tbl-colwidths="[38,44,18]"}
:::

. . .

Question 6 needs one table and a grouping. Questions 1 and 5 are about cause,
and no method on this list answers them alone.

# The simplest integration

## Group on one table, test the other

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
You have already done this.

::: {.incremental}
- On Tuesday, the species table gave every sample a group: anaerobe-dominant or
  *Lactobacillus*-dominant.
- On Wednesday, you tested the gene table against that group:
  **`r scales::comma(n_comm)` genes** differ.
- That is integration. Information from one table organised your analysis of the
  other.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 5
per_sample |>
  filter(time_point == "week_18") |>
  mutate(group = if_else(lacto_fraction >= 0.5, "Lactobacillus-\ndominant", "anaerobe-\ndominant")) |>
  ggplot(aes(lacto_fraction, host_score, colour = group)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal[["orange"]], pal[["teal"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Lactobacillus fraction (species table)",
       y = "inflammatory score (gene table)", title = "Week 18, one dot per sample") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 17) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```
:::
::::

## Grouping throws information away

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
per_sample |>
  filter(time_point == "week_18") |>
  ggplot(aes(lacto_fraction)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, boundary = 0, fill = pal[["grey"]], colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = 2, colour = "grey30") +
  annotate("segment", x = 0.47, xend = 0.53, y = 30, yend = 30, colour = pal[["orange"]],
           linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 33, label = "different groups", colour = pal[["orange"]], size = 5) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0.53, xend = 0.98, y = 45, yend = 45, colour = pal[["navy"]],
           linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.75, y = 48, label = "same group", colour = pal[["navy"]], size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Lactobacillus fraction, week 18", y = "samples") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.incremental}
- 0.49 and 0.51 end up in different groups.
- 0.51 and 0.99 end up in the same group.
- In exchange, you get a sentence you can say: "these genes differ between
  the two kinds of community."
:::

::: {.fragment}
The methods later today keep more of the information, and their results are
harder to put in one sentence.
:::
:::
::::

# Back up: what do we think causes what?

## Draw it before you choose a method {.center}

A **DAG** (directed acyclic graph) is a drawing of what you think causes what.

::: {.incremental}
- A box for each thing, measured or not.
- An arrow means "changing this would change that."
- **A missing arrow is also a claim**: that one thing has no direct effect on
  the other.
:::

. . .

You draw it before you look at the data, from what you know about the biology.

## Let's draw one: preterm birth {.our-turn}

::: {.incremental}
- What did we measure in each table, and where does each thing sit relative to
  preterm birth?
- Which measurements are **causes**, and which are **readouts** of a cause?
- What did we **not** measure that probably matters?
:::

## One version of that drawing

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 6.2
real_nodes <- tribble(
  ~name,      ~x,   ~y,  ~label,                                   ~kind,
  "sex",      0,    3,   "sexual partners,\ndouching",              "unmeasured",
  "abx",      0,    1.6, "antibiotics",                            "unmeasured",
  "ses",      2.2,  4.3, "smoking, income,\nstress",                "unmeasured",
  "micro",    2.2,  2.3, "anaerobic\ncommunity",                   "measured",
  "readout",  2.2,  0.6, "Nugent, pH,\nAmsel criteria",            "measured",
  "inf",      4.6,  2.3, "host\ninflammation",                     "measured",
  "otherinf", 4.6,  0.6, "other infections\n(STIs, UTI)",          "unmeasured",
  "remodel",  6.8,  2.3, "cervical\nremodelling",                  "unmeasured",
  "prior",    6.8,  4.3, "previous preterm\nbirth, cervical\nlength",            "unmeasured",
  "preterm",  9,    2.3, "preterm\nbirth",                         "outcome"
)
real_edges <- tribble(
  ~from,      ~to,
  "sex",      "micro",
  "abx",      "micro",
  "ses",      "micro",
  "ses",      "prior",
  "micro",    "readout",
  "micro",    "inf",
  "otherinf", "inf",
  "inf",      "remodel",
  "remodel",  "preterm",
  "prior",    "preterm"
)
draw_dag(real_nodes, real_edges, wx = 0.85, wy = 0.32)
```

Grey boxes are things nobody in this cohort measured.

## The DAG we used to build the outcome

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 5.8
gen_nodes <- tribble(
  ~name,     ~x,  ~y,  ~label,                                      ~kind,
  "micro",   2,   3,   "anaerobe fraction,\naveraged over 3 visits", "measured",
  "host",    2,   0.8, "host inflammation\n(hidden flag)",           "latent",
  "preterm", 5.5, 1.9, "preterm\nbirth",                            "outcome",
  "readout", 0,   4.3, "16S counts, Nugent,\npH, cytokines",         "measured",
  "genes",   0,   -0.4, "inflammatory genes\nin the gene table",     "measured",
  "batch",   -2.4, -0.4, "RNA\nbatch",                               "measured"
)
gen_edges <- tribble(
  ~from,     ~to,        ~label,
  "micro",   "preterm",  "odds ratio 3",
  "host",    "preterm",  "odds ratio 5.5",
  "micro",   "readout",  NA,
  "host",    "genes",    NA,
  "batch",   "genes",    NA
)
draw_dag(gen_nodes, gen_edges, wx = 0.95, wy = 0.36) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.9, y = 1.9, label = "no arrow:\nindependent\nby design",
           colour = pal[["orange"]], size = 6, fontface = "italic", lineheight = 0.9)
```

The species and genes are real sequencing data. The outcome was built from
these two causes and nothing else.

## So what should combining do?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 5.5
ggplot(person, aes(micro_score, host_score)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = outcome), size = 2.6, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey40", linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = ocol) +
  labs(x = "mean anaerobe fraction (species table)",
       y = "mean inflammatory score\n(gene table)", colour = NULL,
       title = "One dot per person") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
Two causes, no arrow between them. Predict before the next slide: does adding
the second table help?

::: {.fragment}
The two scores correlate at
**`r sprintf("%.2f", cor(person$micro_score, person$host_score))`**.
That is a feature of how we built the data.
:::

::: {.fragment}
In real cohorts, an anaerobic community and an inflamed epithelium are strongly
correlated.
:::
:::
::::

## The DAG predicted the lift

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 6.2
ggplot(rocs, aes(fpr, tpr, colour = model)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey75", linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = mcol, guide = "none") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "false positive rate", y = "true positive rate") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 22)
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
glm(preterm ~ micro_z + host_z,
    family = binomial)
```

::: {.incremental}
- [Species table alone: AUC `r auc_of("microbiome only")`]{style="color: #2a9d8f; font-weight: 600;"}
- [Gene table alone: AUC `r auc_of("host only")`]{style="color: #e76f51; font-weight: 600;"}
- [Both: AUC `r auc_of("both")`]{style="color: #2b3a67; font-weight: 600;"}
:::

::: {.fragment}
Two independent causes, so each table adds something the other cannot.
:::
:::
::::

## In real data, expect a smaller lift

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4.2
med_nodes <- gen_nodes |> filter(name %in% c("micro", "host", "preterm"))
med_edges <- tribble(
  ~from,   ~to,       ~style,
  "micro", "preterm", "solid",
  "host",  "preterm", "solid",
  "micro", "host",    "dashed"
)
draw_dag(med_nodes, med_edges, wx = 0.95, wy = 0.3) +
  expand_limits(x = c(0.6, 6.4)) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.12, y = 1.9, label = "the arrow we left out",
           colour = pal[["orange"]], size = 6.5, fontface = "italic", hjust = 0) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.incremental}
- If anaerobes cause inflammation, part of the microbiome's effect travels
  **through** the host. The gene table then already carries it.
- Adding the species table would add less, even though the bacteria matter.
- "Doesn't improve the prediction" is not the same as "doesn't matter."
:::

## Predictive is not causal

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 5.2
role_col <- c(cause = pal[["navy"]], `readout of a cause` = pal[["teal"]],
              bystander = pal[["gold"]], technical = pal[["grey"]], unrelated = pal[["grey"]])
ranking |>
  mutate(label = fct_reorder(label, auc),
         role = factor(role, names(role_col))) |>
  ggplot(aes(auc, label, colour = role)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = 2, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0.5, xend = auc, yend = label), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = role_col, name = "role in the DAG we used") +
  labs(x = "AUC for preterm birth, one predictor at a time (per person)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

. . .

Rank by AUC and you would call Nugent and IL-1β drivers of preterm birth. In
the model that made these data, neither one does anything.

## Prediction is not mechanism {.center}

::: {.incremental}
- The features a method selects are the ones that **predict** or **move
  together**, not the ones that cause.
- That includes loading plots, top-feature lists and networks.
- Drawing a DAG, and then building a model from it, is how you start to ask
  about cause.
:::

. . .

**Workshop 3 will focus on modelling and uncertainty**, in April 2027.

# A tour of mixOmics

## A good place to learn the rest: [mixomics.org](http://mixomics.org/) {.center}

Most of what follows is a small tour of methods from mixOmics, with a couple of
alternatives that are not on that site.

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}
| method | the question | on mixOmics |
|---|---|---|
| CCA, PLS, sparse PLS | which features move together across two tables? | yes |
| MOFA | what structure is shared, and what belongs to one table? | no |
| STATIS, mixKernel, SNF | which people look alike across every table? | mixKernel is a companion |
| DIABLO | which features from both tables separate the groups? | yes |
| two scores in one model | does the second table add to the prediction? | no |

: {tbl-colwidths="[28,54,18]"}
:::

# Patterns shared by two tables: CCA and PLS

## Find a mix of species and a mix of genes that move together

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5.5
spls_scores |>
  ggplot(aes(species_comp1, genes_comp1, colour = community)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(anaerobe = pal[["orange"]], lactobacillus = pal[["teal"]]),
                      name = "week 18 community") +
  labs(x = "species mix (component 1)", y = "gene mix (component 1)",
       title = "Sparse PLS, one dot per person") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Sparse PLS picks 10 species and 50 genes, and weights them so the two mixes
  rise and fall together across people.
- **No outcome goes in.**
- Coloured afterwards by community: the shared axis is *Lactobacillus* against
  anaerobes.
:::
:::
::::

## CCA chases correlation, PLS chases correlation times spread

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.incremental}
- **CCA** finds the mixes with the highest correlation. With 2,000 genes and
  157 people it can always reach a perfect one, so it needs a penalty
  (regularised CCA).
- **PLS** also rewards a mix whose values spread widely.
- Genes that rise and fall together add up to a big spread, so PLS goes after
  **large groups of co-expressed genes**.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
module_cor |>
  mutate(set = fct_rev(fct_inorder(set))) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean_abs_cor, set, fill = set)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`50 genes sPLS picked` = pal[["navy"]],
                               `50 random genes` = pal[["grey"]])) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", mean_abs_cor)), hjust = -0.2, size = 6) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "average correlation between\ngenes in the set", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```

The genes it picked move together far more than random genes.
:::
::::

## The genes it picks are representatives of a group

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 5.5
stability |>
  mutate(rank = row_number()) |>
  ggplot(aes(rank, freq)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = in_full_fit), width = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[["navy"]], `FALSE` = pal[["grey"]]),
                    labels = c(`TRUE` = "picked in the full data", `FALSE` = "not picked"),
                    name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "genes, most often picked first",
       y = "how often picked in\n50 reruns on resampled people") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.incremental}
- `r nrow(stability)` different genes were picked at least once. None was picked
  every time.
- Among genes that move together, small changes in the data swap which ones
  get picked.
- A gene missing from the list may have lost to a neighbour. Check how it
  correlates with the component.
:::
:::
::::

# MOFA: what is shared, and what belongs to one table

## Factors, and which tables each one lives in

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 5
tribble(
  ~factor,    ~species, ~genes,
  "Factor 1", 0.35,     0.12,
  "Factor 2", 0.00,     0.15,
  "Factor 3", 0.00,     0.08,
  "Factor 4", 0.10,     0.00
) |>
  pivot_longer(-factor, names_to = "table", values_to = "explained") |>
  mutate(table = factor(table, c("species", "genes")), factor = fct_rev(factor)) |>
  ggplot(aes(table, factor, fill = explained)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 2) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f4f4f4", high = pal[["navy"]], guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Variance explained (sketch)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.incremental}
- MOFA (multi-omics factor analysis) is like a PCA run on all the tables at
  once.
- Each factor is an axis of variation across people. MOFA reports how much of
  each table that factor explains.
- **Shared factors** (Factor 1) show up in both tables. **Table-specific
  factors** (Factors 2 to 4) show up in only one.
- There is no outcome inside the model.
:::
:::
::::

## Where MOFA fits

::: {.incremental}
- You test the factors **afterwards** against the outcome, the RNA batch, age and
  visit. A factor that tracks the batch is something to catch, not a finding.
- In our data, the host inflammation lives only in the gene table. MOFA would
  show it as a gene-only factor, next to the shared *Lactobacillus* axis.
- The methods that are built to find shared signal tend to hide a signal that
  lives in one table. DIABLO is one of them.
- MOFA is not part of mixOmics. See [the MOFA site](https://biofam.github.io/MOFA2/)
  for tutorials.
:::

# Another route: compare people, not features

## Each table becomes a map of who looks like whom

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5.5
set.seed(6)
# 16 people: community splits 1-8 from 9-16 (both tables);
# inflammation splits 5-8 and 13-16 from the rest (genes only)
community <- rep(c(1, -1), each = 8)
inflamed <- rep(rep(c(-1, 1), each = 4), 2)
sim_of <- function(p, s_comm, s_infl) {
  x <- outer(community, rnorm(p)) * s_comm + outer(inflamed, rnorm(p)) * s_infl +
    matrix(rnorm(16 * p), 16, p)
  cor(t(x))
}
sims <- list(species = sim_of(30, 1.2, 0), genes = sim_of(200, 0.6, 0.6))
sims$combined <- (sims$species + sims$genes) / 2
sim_tile <- function(m, title) {
  tibble(a = c(row(m)), b = c(col(m)), s = c(m)) |>
    ggplot(aes(a, -b, fill = s)) +
    geom_tile() +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#f4f4f4", mid = "#f4f4f4", high = pal[["navy"]],
                         midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1), guide = "none") +
    coord_equal() +
    labs(title = title) +
    theme_void(base_size = 18) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
}
(sim_tile(sims$species, "species") | sim_tile(sims$genes, "genes")) /
  (plot_spacer() + sim_tile(sims$combined, "combined") + plot_spacer() +
     plot_layout(widths = c(1, 2, 1))) +
  plot_annotation(title = "People × people similarity (sketch)",
                  theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 20, hjust = 0.5)))
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%" style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
::: {.incremental}
- Each table becomes one **people × people** similarity matrix, using any
  distance: UniFrac, Bray–Curtis, correlation.
- The matrices are combined into one:
  - **STATIS / DISTATIS**: a weighted average; tables that agree with the
    others count more.
  - **mixKernel**: the same idea with kernels, from the mixOmics team.
  - **SNF**: shares similarity through each person's nearest neighbours,
    then clusters people.
:::
:::
::::

## Features or people: two places to start

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
| starts from | methods | gives you |
|---|---|---|
| the tables of features | PCA, MOFA, sparse PLS, DIABLO | axes of variation, and a weight for every feature |
| a similarity matrix per table | STATIS, DISTATIS, mixKernel, SNF | a map or clusters of people |

: {tbl-colwidths="[28,36,36]"}
:::

::: {.incremental}
- Starting from people, a table with 2,000 genes and one with 30 species each
  give one matrix, so **the big table does not drown the small one**.
- The price: **features come back only indirectly**, and every person needs
  every table.
- Weighting by agreement turns down a table that tells a different story, and
  that story may be the finding.
:::

# DIABLO: features from both tables that separate the groups

## Two goals, added together

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
DIABLO builds a mix of species and a mix of genes. It scores each pair on:

1. how well each mix **separates preterm from term**, plus
2. how well the two mixes **agree with each other**, times a weight called the
   **design**, from 0 to 1.

::: {.fragment}
At design 0 it fits each table on its own. Higher values push the two tables
toward a shared axis, possibly at the cost of separation.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 4.8
diablo_design |>
  pivot_longer(c(auc, cross_table_cor), names_to = "what", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(what = recode(what, auc = "separates the groups\n(cross-validated AUC)",
                       cross_table_cor = "agreement between\nthe two tables")) |>
  ggplot(aes(design, value, colour = what)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal[["navy"]], pal[["orange"]]), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9)) +
  labs(x = "design", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Here, more agreement cost nothing. In data with a strong signal in only one
table, it can.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Not covered on slides: when both tables are fitted to the same outcome, the
agreement between them is partly just the outcome. To ask whether host and
microbes covary beyond the label, correlate the two mixes within each group.
:::

## With 2,000 genes, any labels separate

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4.6
shuffle_scores |>
  mutate(labels = recode(labels, real = "real labels", shuffled = "labels shuffled at random"),
         labels = fct_relevel(labels, "real labels")) |>
  ggplot(aes(comp1, comp2, colour = label)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~labels, scales = "free") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = ocol, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "component 1", y = "component 2",
       title = "Sparse PLS-DA on the gene table, plotted on the people it was fitted to") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", strip.text = element_text(size = 16))
```

::: {.fragment}
Cross-validated AUC, predicting people the model did not see:
real labels **`r sprintf("%.2f", shuffle_cv$auc[shuffle_cv$labels == "real"])`**,
shuffled labels **`r sprintf("%.2f", shuffle_cv$auc[shuffle_cv$labels == "shuffled"])`**.
Only the cross-validated number tells them apart.
:::

## Loadings are the recipe, not a ranking

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 6
diablo_load |>
  filter(table == "genes") |>
  slice_max(abs(loading), n = 15) |>
  mutate(label = fct_reorder(label, loading)) |>
  ggplot(aes(loading, label, fill = higher_in)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = ocol, name = "higher in") +
  labs(x = "weight on component 1", y = NULL, title = "DIABLO, gene table") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.incremental}
- The bars say **what the component is made of**. IL6, THBD and ORM1 on the
  preterm side: this axis is inflammation, the signal we built in.
- They are **not** the genes that differ most between groups. A gene's bar
  depends on its group of co-expressed neighbours, and on which neighbour won
  the selection.
- For "which genes differ?", use Wednesday's test.
:::
:::
::::

## Did DIABLO beat two numbers in a glm?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
diablo_cv |>
  filter(model != "DIABLO, both tables weighted") |>
  mutate(model = recode(model,
                        `DIABLO, both tables averaged` = "DIABLO, both tables",
                        `DIABLO, species table's vote` = "DIABLO, species only",
                        `DIABLO, gene table's vote` = "DIABLO, genes only"),
         model = fct_reorder(model, auc),
         simple = model == "two scores, one glm") |>
  ggplot(aes(auc, model, colour = simple)) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = auc - 2 * auc_sd, xmax = auc + 2 * auc_sd), height = 0.2) +
  geom_point(size = 4.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[["orange"]], `FALSE` = pal[["navy"]]), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = "cross-validated AUC (10 repeats of 5-fold)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}
```{.r}
# one row per person, values averaged over the 3 visits
glm(preterm ~ anaerobe_fraction + inflammation_score,
    family = binomial)

block.splsda(list(species = clr_species,       # 10% prevalence
                  genes   = top_2000_genes),   # most variable
             outcome, ncomp = 2, design = 0.1,
             keepX = list(species = c(10, 10), genes = c(50, 50)))
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Each table alone: about `r cv_of("DIABLO, species table's vote")`. Together:
  `r cv_of("DIABLO, both tables averaged")`. The tables carry different
  information, as the DAG said.
- Two hand-picked scores in a glm: `r cv_of("two scores, one glm")`.
- The simple model wins, because we gave it what we knew: which gene set
  means inflammation.
:::
:::
::::

## Three things not to conclude

::: {.incremental}
- **"This gene wasn't selected, so it doesn't matter."** It may have lost to a
  co-expressed neighbour.
- **"The species table didn't improve the prediction, so the microbiome doesn't
  matter."** Its effect may already be carried by the genes.
- **"DIABLO separates community types perfectly."** Never use an outcome that was
  built from one of the tables. Community type comes from the species counts, so
  that table separates it by construction.
:::

# What we can and can't claim

## All of them can overfit {.center}

With 157 people and over 2,000 features, you can find a combination that
separates any two groups, as the shuffled labels showed.

. . .

Every number you report should come from people the model did not see:
cross-validation, or better, a separate cohort.

. . .

Any step that looks at the labels, including choosing features or settings,
goes inside the cross-validation.

## Our own result, with its limits

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
- We chose both scores **after** looking at the data all week.
- Fitted and tested on the same people: AUC `r auc_of("both")`, 95% interval
  `r sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", models$auc_lo[models$model == "both"], models$auc_hi[models$model == "both"])`.
- Cross-validated: `r cv_of("two scores, one glm")`.
- We never tested it in a second cohort.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(models, aes(auc, fct_rev(model), colour = model)) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = auc_lo, xmax = auc_hi), height = 0.25, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = mcol, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = "AUC with 95% interval", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 22)
```
:::
::::

::: {.fragment}
The improvement is real. Report its size with the interval, and say how the
scores were chosen.
:::
